exampleAnswers.title: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}.$ What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = 2\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1-\mathbf{b}_2?$
question.explanation:
We are given that

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{c}_1 = 2\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2 \\ \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1-\mathbf{b}_2. \end{cases} \]

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. Adding the equations, we get

\[ \mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2 = 3\mathbf{b}_1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac 1 3\mathbf{c}_2. \]

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[ \mathbf{c}_1 = 2\left( \dfrac 1 3\mathbf{c}_1 + \dfrac 13\mathbf{c}_2\right) + \mathbf{b}_2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_2 = \dfrac 1 3\mathbf{c}_1 - \dfrac 2 3\mathbf{c}_2. \]

Since $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x} &= 6 \mathbf{b}_1 - \mathbf{b}_2 \\[5pt] &= 6\left(\dfrac 1 3\mathbf{c}_1 + \dfrac 1 3 \mathbf{c}_2\right) - \left(\dfrac 1 3 \mathbf{c}_1 - \dfrac 2 3\mathbf{c}_2 \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\mathbf{c}_1 + 2\mathbf{c}_2 - \dfrac 1 3\mathbf{c}_1 + \dfrac 2 3\mathbf{c}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{3}\mathbf{c}_1 + \dfrac{8}{3}\mathbf{c}_2 \end{align*}

Therefore, $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C}=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{3} \\ \dfrac{8}{3} \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1+2\mathbf{b}_2?$
question.explanation:
We are given that

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2 \\ \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1+2\mathbf{b}_2. \end{cases} \]

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. Multiplying the second equation by $-1$ and adding the equations, we get

\[ \mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{b}_2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{c}_2-\mathbf{c}_1. \]

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[ \mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1+ (\mathbf{c}_2 - \mathbf{c}_1) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_1 = 2\mathbf{c}_1 - \mathbf{c}_2. \]

Since $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x} &= 2 \mathbf{b}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2 \\[5pt] &= 2\left(2\mathbf{c}_1 - \mathbf{c}_2\right) + \left( \mathbf{c}_2 - \mathbf{c}_1 \right) \\[5pt] &= 4\mathbf{c}_1 - 2\mathbf{c}_2 + \mathbf{c}_2 - \mathbf{c}_1 \\[5pt] &= 3\mathbf{c}_1 - \mathbf{c}_2 \end{align*}

Therefore, $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C}=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = 3\mathbf{b}_1-2\mathbf{b}_2$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 =- \mathbf{b}_2?$
question.explanation:
We are given that

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{c}_1 = 3\mathbf{b}_1-2\mathbf{b}_2 \\ \mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{b}_2. \end{cases} \]

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. From the second equation, we get

\[ \mathbf{b}_2 = -\mathbf{c}_2. \]

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[ \mathbf{c}_1= 3\mathbf{b}_1-2(-\mathbf{c}_2) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_1 = \dfrac{\mathbf{c}_1 -2 \mathbf{c}_2}{3}. \]

Since $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x} &= 9 \mathbf{b}_1 + 2 \mathbf{b}_2 \\[3pt] &= 9\left (\dfrac{\mathbf{c}_1 -2 \mathbf{c}_2}{3}\right) + 2 ( -\mathbf{c}_2) \\[3pt] &= 3\mathbf{c}_1 - 6\mathbf{c}_2 - 2\mathbf{c}_2 \\[3pt] &= 3 \mathbf{c}_1 -8 \mathbf{c}_2 \end{align*}

Therefore, $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C}=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}.$ What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1-2\mathbf{b}_2$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2?$
question.explanation:
We are given that

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1-2\mathbf{b}_2 \\ \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2. \end{cases} \]

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. Multiplying the second equation by $2$ and adding the equations, we get

\[ \mathbf{c}_1+2\mathbf{c}_2 = 3\mathbf{b}_1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{c}_2. \]

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[ \mathbf{c}_1 = \left( \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{c}_2 \right) - 2\mathbf{b}_2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_2 = -\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_2. \]

Since $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x} &= 2 \mathbf{b_1} - 3 \mathbf{b_2} \\[5pt] &= 2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{c}_2\right) - 3 \left( -\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}_2 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{c}_1+\dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{c}_2 + \mathbf{c}_1 - \mathbf{c}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{3} \mathbf{c}_1 + \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{c}_2 \end{align*}

Therefore, $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C}=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{3} \\ \dfrac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

question.text: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.$ What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = -\mathbf{b}_2$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2 - \mathbf{b}_1?$
question.explanation:
We are given that

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{c}_1 = -\mathbf{b}_2 \\ \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2 - \mathbf{b}_1. \end{cases} \]

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. From the first equation, we get

\[ \mathbf{b}_2 = -\mathbf{c}_1. \]

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

\[ \mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{c}_1 - \mathbf{b}_1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}_1 = -\mathbf{c}_1 - \mathbf{c}_2. \]

Since $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x} &= 3\mathbf{b}_1 + 5 \mathbf{b}_2 \\[3pt] &= 3(-\mathbf{c}_1 -\mathbf{c}_2) + 5\left(-\mathbf{c}_1\right) \\[3pt] &= -3\mathbf{c}_1 - 3\mathbf{c}_2 - 5\mathbf{c}_1 \\[3pt] &= -8\mathbf{c}_1 - 3\mathbf{c}_2 \end{align*}

Therefore, $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C}=\begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$
